7.0.s.en: (1) The answer to the scribes and Pharisees and the rebuke of them

7.0.0.en: "Which came from Jerusalem": for the scribes and Pharisees to leave Jerusalem was unusual ... so we are before a delegation that went to Capernaum to investigate the facts about the phenomenon of this man whose fame had spread and who had drawn thousands to himself, whether by his teaching or his miracles. And feelings of jealousy possessed their hearts, more than their desire to see the truth ... and for this reason the first thing that shocked them was that they saw the disciples of Christ eating bread without washing their hands, and for this reason they condemned them for this action.

7.1.0.en: In these two verses St. Mark gives an important background for the reader of his Gospel, because he was writing for non-Jews about some of the customs of the Pharisees and of the Jews in general, so that the reader might understand why they blamed the disciples in (v. 2), and as an introduction to their conversation with Christ in (v. 5). So he explains to us their concern for outward cleanliness and their counting it as purification, and washing before eating in their houses, or in the case of their buying any produce from the markets, which could not be eaten without washing the hands, and this cleanliness included also all their vessels, and even the beds on which they lay.

7.2.0.en: The delegation asked the Lord Christ about the reason His disciples violated the religious customs that they had received from their forefathers and fathers.

7.3.0.en: The Lord Christ began His answer by rebuking the scribes and Pharisees, reminding them of what Isaiah prophesied about them (Isa 29:13), making clear their hypocrisy, in that their honoring of God is theoretical, they say something with their tongues and what is inside the heart is something else, so their outward worship becomes without benefit, and likewise their teachings are human teachings springing from their own thoughts and not from the Spirit of God the Holy ... And we also would be hypocrites if we were concerned to show people our religiosity, so as to have a good reputation, without having the true good conduct ... or to bring out our virtues and the sins of others, while we allow our hearts to remain far from God.

7.4.0.en: Thus outward worship (hypocrisy) leads a person on a road that separates him from the commandment of God and its true purpose; and Satan misleads him with trivial matters, and gives them first importance, so that he spends all his concern on them, and without knowing it, he is thereby rejecting God Himself.

7.4.1.en: My dear friend ... when God commanded man in the Law to purify himself and wash, this was a reference to purity of heart and thought ... bodily cleanliness is something important, but cleanliness of the heart from jealousy, envy and strife is more important ... so are you careful, before Communion for example, about the purity of your heart and soul, or do you care about the purity of your body? May we examine our thoughts and intentions, and wash them with repentance as we wash our bodies with water.

7.5.0.en: The Lord Christ gives them an example that shows the deviation of their teaching and the corruption of the tradition of their elders ... for while God commanded, in the Law of Moses, the honoring of father and mother (Ex 20:12), and that death should be the punishment for the son who curses either of them, because of the greatness of their standing, likewise in (v. 11), the elders of the Jews came with a strange teaching that contradicts the commandment of God, which is that offering the Corban (gifts) to the temple is more lasting and more binding upon a person than giving it to his needy parents?!! And this tradition is a clear violation of the commandment of honor, and in truth it benefits no one but the elders of the Jews. And so in (v. 12): you prevent people from caring for their parents because of your human teaching, contradicting the command of God. And it is not this teaching only, for there are many other matters by which you have broken the commandment of God, you hypocrites.

7.6.0.en: Christ wanted His words and teaching to be all-embracing, so He directed His speech to the crowd, after He had been addressing the scribes and Pharisees. And to draw their attention, He said to them: "Hearken unto me every one of you, and understand."

7.7.0.en: "There is nothing from without": what is meant by it is foods, whether washed or unwashed, and likewise the hands holding this food.

7.7.1.en: "The things which come out": that is, evil speech, such as condemnation, cursing and lying, and likewise looks of evil lust, for these are what defile the whole man.

7.7.2.en: "... ears to hear, let him hear": an expression that Christ used often to indicate the importance of what He spoke and taught ... and it may also be said that "two ears" means:

7.7.3.en: The first ear: the outer ear that hears.

7.7.4.en: The second ear: the inner will that understands and acts.

7.7.5.en: And the general meaning intended is: the Lord Christ wanted to move people from the literal understanding of the commandment to the depth of its spiritual meaning, for when God spoke of the unclean animals and the clean animals in the Law of Moses, He intended what lies behind that...

7.7.6.en: First: to put a separation between what His people eat and what the pagans eat, so that He keeps His people from mixing or from the worship of the Gentiles.

7.7.7.en: Second: and it is the deeper meaning of this verse, that true purity and uncleanness have their source in the heart and mind of man, and not in what comes to him from outside.

7.8.0.en: "And when he was entered into the house, his disciples asked him": as usual, when something was hard for the disciples, they would ask Christ about it again away from the crowds, and Christ answered with the same meaning explained in the two preceding verses.

7.9.0.en: The explanation here is still directed to Christ's disciples, so He makes clear to them that food does not affect the spiritual condition of man (the heart), which is the basic measure before God, for the waste of the food after its digestion goes out of the body, so the body rids itself of what is harmful, and the intestines absorb from it what is useful, and thus the heart is not affected by foods, but remains pure.

7.10.0.en: The meaning was explained in (vv. 15-16), but the Lord Christ adds here the kinds of sins that come out of the heart and the unclean, evil conscience, such as thoughts of adultery, and thoughts of fornication, that is, licentiousness, murder, theft, covetousness, that is, excessive love of money and of self, and thoughts of wickedness, which means harboring evil toward another, and deceit, which is every kind of trickery, and lasciviousness, meaning the release of all the lusts such as perversion, and the evil eye, which comes in the sense of envy and jealousy or looking at things that stir up base lusts, and blasphemy, and pride, that is, man's self-importance and contempt for others and justifying himself before God, and foolishness. And all these have as their source not food that defiles a man, but an evil heart and mind that defile the whole man, and our allowing the evil thoughts with which Satan speaks to us is a pollution of the heart and mind, so do not open a dialogue with Satan, close the door of discussion with him completely.

7.10.1.en: How wonderful is the spirituality of the rite of the Liturgy of our Church, when the priest prays secretly in outpouring, saying: "Remember, O Lord, my weakness ... and because of my sins in particular and the uncleanness of my heart, do not withhold from Thy people the grace of Thy Holy Spirit." By this prayer the priest expresses the cry of us all to God that He cleanse our hearts and thoughts and intentions before partaking of His divine Mysteries, and it is a spirit of humility that the rite teaches the priest and all of us, and it confirms what Christ taught, that uncleanness has its source in the heart, and nothing washes it but repentance and the Blood of Christ offered on His holy altar.

7.11.0.en: The Lord left the region of Capernaum and went to the parts of Tyre and Sidon (two cities 80 kilometers west of Capernaum, lying on the Mediterranean Sea in present-day Lebanon). And Christ's going there was for more than one reason, the most important being:

7.11.1.en: The first: to get away from the evil and the lying in wait that had become evident from the scribes and Pharisees. The second: His concern for the salvation of the non-Jewish Gentiles ... for Christ's salvation is for all on condition of faith in Him. And although Christ tried not to make Himself known, perhaps to be alone with Himself and His disciples, the news of His arrival had spread.

7.11.2.en: "The coasts of Tyre and Sidon": the word coasts (borders) means boundaries ... and it comes here in the sense of the lands neighboring Tyre and Sidon.

7.12.0.en: "Fell at his feet": it makes clear the bad condition of the woman and the severity of her problem, her hope in Christ, and above all her humility.

7.12.1.en: "A Greek" (a Gentile): this title was applied to non-Jews, and it was a hateful title to them.

7.12.2.en: "A Syrophenician": that is, present-day Lebanon and the region of the Levant, and the name Syria was mentioned to distinguish her from the (Phoenicians of Libya) in North Africa.

7.12.3.en: And the meaning is: when Christ reached this region, this woman, a stranger to the people of Christ, came asking Him for healing for her daughter, whom Satan possessed, of course after she had heard from the crowd about the Lord's miracles, and St. Matthew adds (15:23) to what St. Mark mentioned that she was crying out after Him before He entered the house, and that the disciples asked the Lord to heal her and He did not listen to them at first.

7.13.0.en: The Lord's answer seemed harsh, but by this answer He wanted to make clear the error of the Jews' opinion of the Gentiles, in considering themselves "children" and everyone else "dogs." Likewise the Lord's answer was not lowering the woman's worth in this statement, and He also wanted afterward to make clear the depth of the woman's faith and the extent of her humility. As for her humble reply, and her not objecting or going away, but agreeing to what seemed an insult, it made the Lord bless the steadfastness of her faith and her hope in Him, and respond to her request, and tell her that her daughter was healed and she should go to her ... from which it is clear that His power to crush the demons is very great, for His power surpasses all distances.

7.14.0.en: So the woman did, and returned to her house to find her daughter completely healed, and that the demon had gone out of her. And the phrase "laid upon the bed" means rest and sleeping in peace, and not the result of the raging that had afflicted her at first ... see also the commentary on the same miracle in Mt 15:22-28.

7.14.1.en: My dear friend ... do you not agree with me that the woman's humility and the confidence of her faith were behind the answer to her petition? Read with me, beloved, what the Holy Spirit says about the petition of the humble: "The prayer of the humble pierceth the clouds: and till it come nigh, it will not rest; and it will not depart till the most High shall visit, and judge righteously, and execute judgment" (Sir 35:21).

7.14.2.en: So the humble man is the one whose petition pierces heaven and remains before the throne of God until He answers it ... May we, my God, learn from this woman humility, confidence and importunity.

7.15.s.en: (4) The healing of the deaf man with an impediment in his speech

7.15.0.en: The Lord Jesus' stay in the parts of Tyre and Sidon did not last long, lest the Jews be offended at Him when they saw Him preaching to the Gentiles, so He returned to the east again toward the Sea of Galilee to the Decapolis (spoken of before in ch. 5:20).

7.16.0.en: "And they bring unto him": what is meant of course is the family of the deaf man who had an impediment in his speech, that is, the deaf and dumb, and as is known, one born deaf cannot learn to speak, and so becomes dumb. And the symbolic meaning of this illness is that the man who does not hear the word of God also becomes dumb in the truth and in witnessing to His name. "To put his hand upon him": a reference to their hope of the healing of the sick man by the mere touch of the Lord.

7.17.0.en: The Lord took this sick man aside, out of concern for him, for Christ cares for all His people and His Church. But each one of us has a special place in His heart. So remember, beloved, that when you are alone with Christ in your inner chamber, He is yours and you are His.

7.17.1.en: What the Lord Jesus did in this miracle:

7.17.2.en: a) "Put his fingers into his ears": that is, He touched his ears. And of course the deaf and dumb man cannot hear or understand, but he can distinguish the touch that means love and compassion.

7.17.3.en: b) "He spit, and touched his tongue": that is, He put His finger on his tongue, then took of His spittle and touched the tongue of the dumb man, to show that the power of healing was going forth from Him.

7.17.4.en: c) "Looking up to heaven": to declare that He and the Father are one, and to teach us that heaven is our help. d) "He sighed": that is, He uttered a deep sound like a groan, by which He expressed His pain and tenderness toward this man before his healing.

7.17.5.en: e) "And saith unto him": that is, He commanded him by His authority alone.

7.17.6.en: f) "Ephphatha": that is, "Be opened," and what is meant by that is the ears and the tongue together.

7.18.0.en: Straightway, that is, at once, the healing took place, "and he spake plain," that is, the speech came from his lips sound like that of one accustomed to speech from his childhood, for God always does a perfect work in the life of man. "He charged them that they should tell no man": Christ asked, in His humility and in His flight from the glory of men, which He does not accept, the family of the one who was healed and the crowd not to spread the news of the miracle. But, as much as He charged them, they did the opposite, for "so much the more a great deal they published it," that is, they spread it completely, in a state of amazement, confessing that all the works of Christ were good.

7.18.1.en: "He maketh both the deaf to hear, and the dumb to speak": the use of the plural form here indicates that there were other miracles for the deaf and the dumb, but they were not all mentioned...

7.18.2.en: My beloved God ... loose my tongue with Your praise and thanksgiving in my prayer ... make me speak with You always about everything and all the time ... open my ears to hear and respond to Your repeated calls, for how sweet is the hearing of Your voice, and how good is speaking with You!!

7.18.3.en: Chapter 8: the feeding of the crowds, the hypocrisy of the Pharisees, the healing of the blind man, the foretelling of death and resurrection

8.0.s.en: (1) The feeding of the crowds with the seven loaves

8.0.0.en: "Dalmanutha": a small, little-known village on the Sea of Galilee, near "Magdala," the town of Mary Magdalene.

8.1.s.en: (2) Christ's warning against the hypocrisy of the Pharisees

8.1.0.en: "And the Pharisees came forth": an expression that St. Mark intended to show that they were like cunning foxes, which had been hiding, and then came out to get at their prey.

8.1.1.en: "Began to question with him ... tempting him": it also shows us that the purpose of the questioning was not benefit and learning, but the hunting of faults.

8.1.2.en: "And he sighed deeply in his spirit": that is, the Lord grieved and was sorry over their state and their bad intention, and refused to do a miracle for them, for it was fitting for them to believe in everything He had already done, and to turn to their function of teaching the people instead of tempting Christ.

8.1.3.en: "He left them ... and departed": the Lord Christ teaches us an important lesson, which is not to waste our time with the many provokers who seek nothing but argument and useless chatter, but consume our energy and effort for nothing ... so beware, beloved, of these.

8.2.0.en: In the haste of their affairs, the disciples forgot to take bread with them, and they had in the ship only one loaf. And St. Mark mentioned this as an introduction to the disciples' misunderstanding of Christ's meaning in (vv. 15-16).

8.3.0.en: In the ship, Christ began to warn the disciples against the hypocrisy of the Pharisees (Mt 12:1) and the leaven of the wicked Herod, and described their hypocrisy as the malignant leaven buried in the dough, whose evil is not apparent, but is spreading. But the disciples understood that Christ was speaking about bread (leaven), so they remembered their forgetting to buy bread for their food.

8.4.0.en: The Lord knew their talk and their limited understanding, so He asked them, in rebuke, seven questions, which He directs to us also after all He has done with us:

8.4.1.en: Q1: "Why reason ye, because ye have no bread?" What is the reason for the intense thinking about bread, "material things"? (Answer: because we are not yet spiritual.

8.4.2.en: Q2: "Perceive ye not yet?!" Why do your feelings not move with love toward Me? (Answer: because we love many things ... more than You, O Lord!!

8.4.3.en: Q3: "Neither understand?" Where are your minds after all My works? (Answer: our minds are full of the thoughts of this world.

8.4.4.en: Q4: "Have ye your heart yet hardened?" How much time is needed for your hearts to be moved to repentance? (Q5:

8.4.5.en: its meaning? (Answer: a very long time!!!

8.4.6.en: "Having eyes, see ye not?" Do you grieve over everything you see? (Answer: no, for often superficiality takes hold of us and we do not understand the depth of Your purposes. "And having ears, hear ye not?" Do you forget My sayings like this? Q6:

8.4.7.en: and My commandments and My teaching? (Answer: our memory also is superficial, O Lord.

8.4.8.en: "How many baskets full of fragments ... and how many baskets full of fragments Q7:

8.4.9.en: took ye up?" Does the repetition of My work with you have its effect in increasing your faith in Me?! (Answer: yes, O Lord, for if we remember we shall believe, and our confidence will increase and we shall be encouraged, and we shall not again fear any apparent lack, for You will make it up for us.

8.5.0.en: "How is it that ye do not understand?": this is the last reproach, with which the Lord sums up all that went before, that our failure to understand always has its basis in man's forgetting the work of God in his life.

8.5.1.en: Help us then, O my God, not to forget, and visit us always with Your love, and prolong Your longsuffering toward us ... for if we forget, You do not forget us, but continue Your mercies to us as a mother prolongs her patience with her little ones...

8.6.s.en: (3) The healing of the blind man in two stages

8.6.0.en: "Bethsaida": a village at the north of the Sea of Galilee on both banks of the river Jordan, and it is the town of Andrew, Peter and Philip, where they brought to Him a blind man (his relatives), believing, like the faith of the woman with the issue of blood, that Christ would touch and he would be healed.

8.7.0.en: "He took the blind man by the hand": a figure of the fact that Christ takes mankind by the hand so that it does not fall into sin, because: "If the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch" (Mt 15:14).

8.7.1.en: "Led him out of the town": the town signifies the crowding of the world, so a person must take himself out of his daily occupations so that he can be alone with God and be pained in his works.

8.7.2.en: As for the direct meaning of leading him out, it is, first: that Christ does not seek fame or glory from men. Second: a reference to the faith and hope of the blind man, which made Christ, though a stranger to him, lead him. "Spit": an act that Christ used more than once in miracles of healing, and the purpose of it is that He gives and grants healing from within Himself, that is, His essence, that is, the authority of His divinity.

8.7.3.en: "Put his hands upon him": to make him feel secure; and this is the overflow of Christ's constant tenderness toward us ... may we feel that we deserve it!

8.7.4.en: "He asked him if he saw ought": Christ has no need to ask anyone, for He knows everything, but He did this to teach us that he who asks learns, for how many are the things that God hides from the wise and prudent, and reveals unto babes (Lk 10:21).

8.8.0.en: When Christ asked him about his ability to see, he answered that he now saw partially, men as trees. And this healing in stages is a reference to gradual growth in the spiritual life, and the repentance after which man sees things clearly.

8.8.1.en: And this teaches us, if we are servants, to be gentle with the penitents returning to the bosom of the Church, for perhaps all the truths of the faith are not yet clear to them, but they are beloved to the heart of God, and they may precede us into the Kingdom.

8.9.0.en: Christ then touched his eyes to complete his healing ... as if saying to us all, and to everyone who has begun the journey of spiritual healing: My hand is with you to support you and to complete your healing, and to give you complete spiritual insight so that you can discern all things.

8.9.1.en: And as was Christ's custom, He commanded him not to tell anyone of this miracle, to confirm His flight from the praise of men ... and to teach us to hide the good deeds that God has given us to do.

8.10.0.en: "Caesarea Philippi": a city in northern Galilee where there was pagan worship of one of the gods of the Greeks, and its present name is "Banias." In the time of Christ, Philip the son of Herod the Great rebuilt it, and named it "Caesarea" as a courtesy to Caesar of Rome, so it bore his name and became "Caesarea Philippi."

8.10.1.en: On the way from Galilee to the region of Caesarea Philippi, He asked His disciples, saying to them: "Whom do men say that I am?" And their answer differed according to what each of them had heard, for some people claimed that He was John whom God raised after his killing (and this was the opinion of Herod himself), and others said He was Elijah who precedes the Christ according to the prophecy of Malachi: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the day of the LORD" (Mal 4:5), and the saying of St. Mark here agrees with what St. Matthew mentioned (16:14) that others said He was Jeremiah or one of the prophets risen from the dead.

8.11.0.en: Christ asked the disciples a second question completing His previous question, which was: But whom say ye that I am? And Peter answered that He is the Christ Himself, the hope of the whole world. And St. Matthew added (16:17) to what St. Mark mentioned here two things: a) Christ's praise of Peter that he uttered this truth of the faith. b) the declaration that it was not possible for Peter to know this truth except by a revelation from heaven (the Holy Spirit) to him; see the commentary on (Mt 16:16-17). But Christ charged His disciples that they should tell no man of this secret, for His hour had not yet come, and the time for declaring His glory after His crucifixion had not yet come.

8.11.1.en: My beloved brother ... the situation of the Jews' giving their opinion of the person of Christ, that He was Elijah or Jeremiah or another prophet, reminds us of the situation of many of us in these days, for a person sees God as he wants God to be, and not God in His complete reality ... for some see God as merciful without justice, and others see Him as a harsh judge without mercy ... but our Church teaches us, by spiritual balance, to see God through all His attributes and commandments, for He is the merciful and the just, the good and the decisive together, and how dangerous it is to rely on one attribute or one verse that describes God.

8.12.s.en: (5) The foretelling of death and resurrection

8.12.0.en: After Peter and the disciples acknowledged that Jesus is the awaited Christ and the hope of the Gentiles, Christ began to tell them what was to be expected of the plotting of the leaders of the Jews and their priests and His being handed over, and that He would go through many sufferings, beginning with His trial until His crucifixion and death, and then His resurrection on the third day. But these words did not please Peter, who took Christ aside, and began to rebuke Him strongly for what He had said. And at this time Peter did not care about what Christ desired, but on the contrary, rushed after his natural human feelings, and did not see in Christ the suffering Servant of whom Isaiah prophesied (Isa 53:2-3), for the Christian life often means hard work and deprivation and deep suffering ... so fix your gaze on the resurrection that follows the Cross.

8.13.0.en: "But when he had turned about and looked on his disciples": before Christ directed His rebuke to Peter, He looked at His disciples so that His words might be directed to everyone who shared Peter's limited thinking. As for the severe rebuke of Peter, it came as a result of the limitation of his understanding of Christ's redemption of the world, for his concern was confined to the earthly kingship of Christ, and that is the concern of most people, and not the concern of God for the salvation of men.

8.13.1.en: "Satan": despite the difficulty of the word, Christ intended by it to affirm that there is no one who wants to hinder the redemption except Satan himself.

8.14.0.en: The speech here is directed to the disciples, and the Church, and all believers after them. Whoever wants to follow Christ must accept the idea of bearing the cross, and the acceptance of suffering from persecution and leaving family and friends and other things, and no one can do this unless he denies himself (his own self), and humbles himself in true love before his Lord, who went through suffering first.

8.14.1.en: And Christ affirms that the salvation of the soul requires of it striving and leaving material luxury and its selfishness and its lusts, which are obstacles to its salvation, and that it set out in service and preaching, and this will be the way of its deliverance ... for nothing compares with what it will gain with Christ.

8.15.0.en: Christ is still directing His speech to us all, and warns us that all the material gains of the world we shall find hollow and empty, not equal to the loss of the soul and its destruction, and that all the wealth of the world, if a man offered it, would not redeem his soul, whose price is the Blood of Christ alone ... for by following Christ we know the meaning of true life while we are on earth, and we shall have eternal life also...

8.16.0.en: Everyone who neglects Christ's words here, or is ashamed of His sufferings and His Cross, will have no place or share in His Kingdom at His Second Coming...

8.16.1.en: My beloved Lord ... in many cases I find myself refusing suffering and persecution and the way of the Cross, and I do not know that in this way I refuse You, and lose my portion with You ... teach me, my Lord, and reveal to my eyes and heart the lowliness of this world and all its material things, so that I set out toward You, caring for nothing but to follow Your steps, imitating You, so as to please Your heart first, and win my crown in Your Kingdom ... Amen. (ch. 9:1):

8.16.2.en: And He said unto them: "Verily I say unto you, That there be some of them that stand here, which shall not taste of death, till they have seen the kingdom of God come with power."

8.16.3.en: "Them that stand here": that is, some of the disciples will not die before they see the signs of the beginning of the Kingdom of God and its spread with power, by the spread of the preaching and the Gentiles' acceptance of the faith, and the clear marks of the Church, for the Kingdom of God means that God reigns over the hearts of the people who believe in His name...

8.16.4.en: The Transfiguration, the healing of a demoniac, a conversation with the disciples
